books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Figures from Barron’s Premium AP U.S. History 2027, Chapter 7 (about $2.6 billion borrowed, about $400 million from individual savers; Legal Tender Acts 1862–1863; National Bank Acts 1863–1864; first income tax 1861) and the Gilder Lehrman Institute (about $450 million in greenbacks issued). Figures are rounded.
stimulus.text:
How the Union paid for the war (approximate figures).

| Measure | What happened |
| Borrowing | About $2.6 billion in bonds sold; about $400 million of the bonds were bought by individual savers |
| Greenbacks | About $450 million in paper money issued under the Legal Tender Acts of 1862–1863 |
| Taxes | First federal income tax levied in 1861; rates stayed modest |
| National banking | National Bank Acts of 1863–1864 created a national banking system |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Union paid for the war mostly by borrowing and taxing, while the Confederacy printed money until prices soared and by 1863 accepted grain and livestock in place of money. That contrast best shows that the Union’s advantage lay in

options.text: its refusal to print any paper money at all during the whole war.
options.misconception: Background: the Union printed about 450 million dollars in greenbacks; it printed money, but far less recklessly than the Confederacy.

options.text: its stronger credit and taxes, which let it borrow far more than the Confederacy.
its decision to tax only the South, and never its own loyal citizens.
options.misconception: Background: the Union taxed its own loyal citizens; it could not tax the Confederacy.

options.text: its larger enslaved labor force working on Northern farms.
options.misconception: Background: the Union’s advantage was financial, and its enslaved labor force was far smaller than the Confederacy’s.

rationales.A: Background: the Union printed about 450 million dollars in greenbacks; it printed money, but far less recklessly than the Confederacy.
rationales.C: Background: the Union taxed its own loyal citizens; it could not tax the Confederacy.
rationales.D: Background: the Union’s advantage was financial, and its enslaved labor force was far smaller than the Confederacy’s.
rationales.B: The Union could borrow about 2.6 billion dollars because lenders trusted its credit and its tax system, while the Confederacy could only print money until it lost its value.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two treasuries side by side: one borrows, the other prints.
2. Borrowing works only when lenders believe they will be repaid.
3. Background: the Union had an established Treasury, working taxes, and the credit to sell bonds.
4. Background: the Confederacy, cut off from trade, printed until prices soared and money stopped working.
Remember: in a long war, credit is a weapon, and the side that can borrow can keep fighting.
